cues.text: MIT 8111, Ethics and Legal Issues in Information Technology.
Study Session 3: Ethics in Software Development and Data Ownership.
We begin with the first chapter of this session: the ethical foundations in software.
Let us start with a simple but powerful idea.
Ethics evaluates what should be done, not merely what can be built.
Think about that for a moment.
As a software developer, you will often be able to build something.
The ethical question is different: should you build it, and how should you build it?
This is why we distinguish ethics from legal compliance.
Legal compliance is a minimum enforceable standard.
It is the floor, the least that you must do, and it is backed by enforcement.
Ethical practice goes further.
It also considers foreseeable harm, autonomy, inclusion and trust.

So a system could satisfy the minimum legal standard and still fall short ethically, if it ignores harms that could reasonably be foreseen, overrides people's ability to choose, shuts people out, or erodes trust.
Why does this matter so much in software?
Because a software developer's choices shape access to services, decisions, safety and power.
What a system allows, who it serves, how it decides, and who it leaves out are all outcomes of choices made by people building it.
And responsibility does not stop at writing correct code.
It extends to requirements, to deployment, to operations and to retirement.
In other words, it covers the whole life of the software, from deciding what it should do, to putting it into use, to running it, and finally to taking it out of service.
Now let us look at the core principles.
There are eight, and I will take them in order.
First, non-maleficence.
This means avoiding foreseeable harm.
The key word is foreseeable: the duty is to anticipate and avoid harm that a reasonable developer could see coming.
Second, beneficence.
This means promoting welfare and useful outcomes.
Where non-maleficence asks you to avoid doing harm, beneficence asks you to do good, to make the software actually useful to people.
Third, autonomy.
This means respecting informed choices and meaningful control.
People should be able to make choices that are informed, and the control they are given should be meaningful, not merely nominal.
Fourth, justice, also called fairness.
This means distributing benefits and burdens equitably, and avoiding discrimination.
Ask who gains from a system and who carries its costs, and whether that split is fair.
Fifth, transparency and explainability.
This means communicating material processing and decision logic appropriately.
People affected by a system should be told about processing that matters, and about the logic behind its decisions, in a way suited to the audience and the situation.
Sixth, accountability.
This means assigning responsibility, recording decisions and providing remedies.
Someone must be answerable, decisions must be documented, and when things go wrong there must be a way to put them right.
Seventh, privacy, security and data stewardship.
This means protecting information throughout its lifecycle, from the point it is collected through to the end of its use.
Eighth, accessibility and inclusion.
This means designing for diverse abilities, languages, devices and contexts.
Your users will not all have the same abilities, speak the same language, own the same devices or work in the same circumstances.
Let me close the chapter with a distinction that is often confused: equality versus equity.
Equality means identical treatment.
Equity addresses differing barriers, so that people can actually participate.
Here is the example.
Imagine a mandatory high-speed smartphone workflow, where everyone must complete a process using a fast connection on a smartphone.
It can formally treat everyone alike, since every person faces the same requirement.
Yet it excludes people without reliable connectivity.
Identical treatment, then, produces unequal results.
Equity looks at the barriers people actually face.
This is why inclusive design matters.
Inclusive design recognises context, and it involves affected people in requirements and testing.
In other words, you do not guess what barriers people face.
You bring the people who are affected into the process, at the stage where requirements are set and again when the system is tested.
